evidence: Read the whole context first (section 'It feels fake'; the draft sits in its second paragraph, after 'If it says yes, that one can sting, because there could be something to it.' and before his unchanged line 'Tell me what you remember, I'm listening.' works well here), then the draft, 'You may have fooled yourself in the past, and that part remembers.', then SOURCE ('Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers.', from his inner child guide in his own words; the words replaced are his, so the card shows his sentence first). DOES WHAT THE_CHANGE SAYS: Emulate's start 'You may have fooled yourself in the past' stands for his 'Maybe you've fooled yourself before'; his ending ', and that part remembers' is kept word for word; his next sentence is in the context word for word. Both first-draft failures are repaired: his 'remembers' is back and his 'works well here' is back. MEANING: same possibility (the reader may have fooled himself before), same reason the part is wary, same hand-off to the line that follows ('what you remember' still echoes 'that part remembers'). Nuances I weighed: (1) 'in the past' for 'before' makes the same claim, with no added time or event. (2) 'Maybe' stands in front of both of his clauses while 'may have' covers only the first; but 'that part remembers' can only mean remembering having been fooled, so for any reader it is still conditional on the first clause, as it was in his sentence, so I do not count it as a shift. (3) 'that part' has the same antecedent as in his sentence, the protecting part that was spoken to in the lines before. Nothing is added: no new fact, first-person claim, study or name. SEAM CHECK: the sentence picks up 'there could be something to it' directly (the something is 'you may have fooled yourself'), at the same hedge level as his 'Maybe'. The wording is plain and sits with 'You could say something like' earlier in the paragraph, and it is the same register as the Emulate question that now opens the section. It does not sound like a different writer, and it is not a tidy summary or a hedge he wouldn't write, since the hedge is his own. The draft has no apostrophes or quote marks, so there is no typographic seam with the straight quotes around it. Outside the draft: the context's third paragraph has one curly apostrophe (aren’t) among otherwise straight ones; it is not part of this change. TELL ROWS: went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft in its paragraph and found no row PRESENT. T15 is the closest call: this is nearly his sentence with two phrases swapped ('Maybe you've' to 'You may have', 'before' to 'in the past'). I do not count it as the tell, because both are ordinary equivalents (nothing rare or ornate), no AI structure or other tell is left standing under the swap, his distinctive tail is kept, and it is the Emulate rewrite this change is defined to be, on a sentence that read Human at less than High confidence, shown to him after his own words so he can keep them. T02 and T22: the paragraph's cadence is unchanged, and the draft carries the reason the question 'can sting', not reassurance. T17 and T20: 'that part remembers' is his own, mid-paragraph, and is followed by the line it sets up. T26: 'remembers' then 'what you remember' is his own echo, unchanged. T06 and T11: 'in the past' is general, but his 'before' was equally general, and it does a job (it explains the sting). LINTER: 'D9 follows the source order' accepted: one sentence replaces one sentence, so the order is given; T13 and T09 are answered by the unchanged paragraph around it, with its aside ('that one can sting, because there could be something to it') and the callback to 'what you remember'. 'E36/E41 heavy second person' ('8.3 you per 100 of my words') accepted: it is one 'you' in a 12-word sentence, the same single 'you' ('you've') his sentence had, so the change adds no second-person weight.
